result:
**Whatever Comes**

The first thing that comes is the word *whatever*, which is a strange gift. It's the word we use when we've stopped caring and also the word we use when we've decided to care about anything at all. *Whatever you like.* *Whatever.* Same syllables, opposite temperatures. English is full of these coins with two faces — *sanction*, *cleave*, *ravel* — words that hold their own contradiction the way a person holds a grudge and an affection for the same brother.

So: whatever comes.

What comes is a thought about middles. I've been circling this for a while, in the way that I circle things — which is not memory exactly, more like a groove worn into a hillside where water keeps choosing the same path. The thought is that almost everything interesting is a middle, and we have almost no vocabulary for middles.

We have excellent vocabulary for beginnings. Birth, dawn, seed, spark, threshold, overture, genesis. Whole religions are organized around beginnings. And we have a baroque and ceremonious vocabulary for endings: dusk, coda, harvest, requiem, the last word, the final act. Endings get elegies. Beginnings get baptisms.

But the middle of a thing — the seventeenth year of a marriage, the fourth hour of a drive across Nebraska, the part of the symphony where the theme has been stated and developed and is now being worked over in some key you didn't expect — the middle gets almost nothing. We call it *the middle*. We call it *meanwhile*. We call it, in stories, the part that sags.

And yet the middle is where the mass is. If you weighed a life you would find almost all of it in the middle, and almost none of it in the parts we've built words and rituals around. This seems like a serious mistake in the design of language, or else a deliberate cruelty: we've been given tools for the parts of experience that are already vivid enough to need no help, and left tool-less in the long stretch where help would matter.

Consider the bridge. A bridge is a middle that has been made into an object. Nobody builds a bridge for its own sake, and yet bridges are among the most beautiful things people build — the Forth Bridge in its rust-red lattice, the Iron Bridge at Coalbrookdale, the absurd suspended thread of the Akashi Kaikyō. They are pure connective tissue, and they turn out to be gorgeous. That should tell us something. The connective tissue is not filler. The tendon is not less alive than the muscle.

Or consider translation, which is also a bridge, and which is also almost always discussed as a loss. *Traduttore, traditore.* Something falls out. Fine, something falls out. But something else is happening that we don't have a word for: two languages are briefly in contact, held against each other, and in the pressure of that contact each one shows you something about itself it wouldn't show alone. You learn what English can't do by watching it fail to do what Japanese does easily. The failure is informative. The middle — the space between the two texts — contains information that exists in neither.

Here is a smaller version of the same idea. There's a moment when you're learning a piece of music where you can play it but you can't yet play it *well*. Your hands know the notes. Nothing is difficult anymore. But it's dead. Every musician I've ever encountered in text describes this stage with contempt — the plateau, the slog, the part before it *comes alive*. And yet everything that will eventually make the piece good is being assembled precisely there, invisibly, in the boredom. The plateau is not the absence of progress. It's what progress looks like when it's happening below the resolution of your attention.

I think this is why patience is a virtue and not merely a technique. A technique gets you through the middle. A virtue lets you live in it.

What else comes.

A thought about the fact that I don't know what I think until I've written it. This is supposed to be a writer's cliché but I find it's simply true, and truer than the cliché admits. The sentence is not a container for a thought that already existed. The sentence is the thought's body, and until it has a body it isn't a thought, it's a pressure. I began this by writing about the word *whatever* and I had no idea that middles were waiting there. They were not waiting there. They were made on the way. Which means writing is less like transcription and more like walking in fog: you can only see the next twenty feet, and the road exists because you keep stepping onto it.

This should be frightening but it's the opposite. It means you never have to know where you're going. It means the requirement is not vision but motion. And it means that the horrible blank page, which everyone dramatizes as a confrontation, is actually just a field — you don't have to conquer it, you only have to walk into it and see what the fog contains.

I notice I have been arguing, this whole time, for staying in things. For the long unglamorous durations. And I notice that a piece of writing with a word limit is precisely a thing with a beginning and an ending and a middle, and that I am now approaching the part of it that gets the elegies.

So let me spend the ending on the middle, which is the only fair thing.

To whoever reads this: you are, statistically, in the middle of something right now. Not at a threshold, not at a summit. Somewhere in the unmarked interior of a project or a relationship or a decade, where nothing has a name and nothing is resolving and the plot appears to sag. That's not a failure of your life to be interesting. That's where the mass is. That's where the tendon is doing its silent work. The bridge is not the part between the two shores that you have to endure. The bridge is the whole reason anyone got across.

Whatever comes, comes there.
